## Outline (5 minutes)

**1. The August bug (0:00–1:15)**
Tell it plainly for the non-engineers: an AI-written database change removed a safety rule, nothing broke immediately, numbers slowly stopped matching, three weeks to trace, and the person who merged it couldn't explain it. Don't name them. Land on: that last part is the problem, not the AI.

**2. What it revealed: the cost moved (1:15–2:30)**
Writing code got fast. Reviewing it didn't. Numbers: PRs up about 60% since spring; two senior engineers' review time went from roughly 4 hours a week to 11, each. Translate for sales/ops/compliance: our most experienced people now spend a day and a half a week reading code they didn't write, and the backlog of unread code is where the next August bug lives. We've been counting the speedup and not the bill.

**3. The question isn't "should we use AI" (2:30–3:00)**
Say it directly: we're going to keep using these tools. The question is who answers for what they produce. Right now the honest answer is: it's unclear, and nobody's talking about it.

**4. The three rules (3:00–4:15)**
- Author owns every line. If you merge it, you can explain it.
- "The AI wrote it" is never an excuse in a postmortem. Same standard as "I copied it from somewhere."
- PRs over 400 changed lines get split. Not to slow anyone down — so that reviews are something a person can actually do.
One sentence each on why it's fair: these are the standards we'd apply to a contractor or a library, and the tool doesn't get a lower bar.

**5. The ask (4:15–5:00)**
What you want from this room: engineers, start now; leads, enforce it in review; everyone else, this is why you'll hear "no" or "split this" more often, and it's the system working. Close by returning to August: the goal is that next time, the person who merged it can tell you what it did.

## Opening paragraph

In August, one of our engineers merged a database change that an AI assistant had written. Buried in it was a line that quietly removed a safety rule, the kind that says a particular field can never be left empty. Nothing broke that day. Nothing broke that week. What happened instead is that two sets of our numbers slowly stopped agreeing, and it took three weeks to trace that back to one line in one change. When we found it and asked the engineer who merged it what the change actually did, the honest answer was that they didn't know. I want to be clear about why I'm telling this story. It's not a story about AI being bad at writing code. It's a story about a change going into our system that nobody understood, and about the fact that we didn't have a clear answer for whose job it was to understand it. We're not going to stop using these tools. But we need to decide who's responsible for what they produce, and I'd like us to decide that today.

# January 1 Isn't Going to Change Your Life

Every December, we seem to go through the same ritual. We reflect on everything we didn't do, make a mental list of everything we want to change, and convince ourselves that this time will be different. We'll wake up earlier, exercise regularly, read more books, spend less time on our phones, and somehow become a completely different person by February.

And then February arrives.

I have always found the idea of New Year's resolutions a little strange. Why January 1? What is it about a particular date on the calendar that makes us believe we're suddenly more capable of changing our lives?

Don't get me wrong. There's nothing inherently wrong with setting goals or wanting to improve yourself. But I think we've attached too much importance to the idea of a fresh start. We convince ourselves that the beginning of a new year offers some magical opportunity to reinvent ourselves, when, in reality, we're the same people we were on December 31.

The problem, perhaps, isn't that we lack ambition. It's that we keep waiting for the perfect moment to act on it.

We treat personal growth like an annual event rather than an ongoing process. We make ambitious promises to ourselves when motivation is high, only to abandon them when everyday life inevitably gets in the way. And when we miss a day, skip a workout, or fall back into an old habit, we often consider the entire resolution a failure.

But why should missing a week mean abandoning a year?

I think there's something liberating about accepting that change doesn't need a deadline. You don't need January 1 to start reading more. You don't need a Monday to start exercising. And you certainly don't need an entire new year to decide that something in your life deserves to be different.

Maybe we should stop treating January as an opportunity to become someone new and start treating every ordinary Tuesday as an opportunity to become a little better.

There's no countdown, no grand announcement, and no need to wait for the next chapter of the calendar.

Because ultimately, the calendar doesn't change you. What you do with the days on it does.

## The Problem With January 1st

I've made a few New Year's resolutions. I can't tell you what most of them were. That's not a confession, it's the whole point.

The usual explanation for why resolutions fail is that they're badly built. Too vague, too big, no plan. Set smaller goals, track them, stack them onto habits you already have. All true, probably. But it skips over something stranger: why are we all trying to change on the same day?

Every other decision to change comes from somewhere. You start running because your knees ache going up the stairs. You quit something because you catch your reflection and don't like it. You save money because the account hit a number that scared you. The change has a cause, and the cause arrived first.

New Year's Day reverses that. The date shows up and demands a reason. So you go looking for one, and you find something plausible: read more, drink less, call people back. It sounds like a goal. It's really just an answer to the question "well, what are you going to do?"

Nothing in your life has shifted between December 31st and January 1st. Your schedule is the same. The things that made the old habit easy are all still there. The only thing that's different is the calendar, and the calendar has never once stopped anyone from doing anything.

This is why forgetting them is so easy. There's nothing to remember them by. A change you made because of a real moment has that moment attached to it — you can go back to it when you waver. A change you made because it was January has January attached to it, and by the third week that's gone.

I don't think the fix is better resolutions. I think it's noticing that the ones that stick tend to start on unremarkable days, for reasons you didn't choose and couldn't have scheduled. Some Tuesday in March you'll be fed up with something, and that will do more than any list written on a hangover with a pen you had to search for.

So if you've already forgotten what you resolved this year, maybe don't feel bad. You didn't fail at a resolution. You just found out it was never really yours. The real one is coming. It just doesn't know the date yet.

# Why most New Year's resolutions fail (and the one of mine that didn't)

Every January most of us pick something and quit it by February. I don't think that's a character flaw. I think most resolutions are built in a way that makes quitting easy, and the fix is in the design, not the person.

Here's what usually goes wrong.

**1. The goal is a direction, not a thing you do.** "Get fit." "Read more." "Learn a language." You can't do "learn a language" on a Tuesday. Until the resolution becomes a specific action of a specific size, one lesson, one chapter, one walk, there's nothing to actually start, so you don't.

**2. It's sized for January-you.** On the first of the month you're rested and keen, so you plan for someone with an hour a day and no bad weeks. Then February happens. A resolution that only works when you're at your best won't survive the first ordinary week.

**3. Nobody would notice if you stopped.** This is the big one, and it's the one the Welsh thing taught me. Most resolutions are private. You tell no one, or you tell people once and they forget. So when you miss a day, the only person who knows is you, and you are very easy to talk round.

**4. There's no plan for the first slip.** The first missed day feels like the end because the plan never had a line for what happens after a miss. One day off becomes "well, that's over," and the whole thing folds.

## The one that stuck

I've been learning Welsh on an app for 700 days straight. I don't think that's because I'm unusually disciplined. It's because my 12-year-old does it too, and at dinner we check each other's streaks.

Look at that against the list. The action is small and specific: open the app, keep the streak alive. It fits a bad day. And the check isn't something I have to remember to do. It just happens, at a table I'm already sitting at, with someone who will absolutely notice if my number didn't go up. I don't have to supply the willpower. The setup supplies it.

So if you're picking a resolution this year, skip the dramatic one and ask three questions instead. What's the smallest version I'd do on a rough day? Who's going to see whether I did it? And when does that check happen, not "sometime," but a specific spot that's already in your week?

Get those three right and you don't need to be a better person in January. You just need a better setup.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail

Every year, as December comes to an end, we find ourselves making promises to a future version of ourselves. We'll go to the gym, read more books, spend less time on our phones, eat healthier, or finally learn that skill we've been putting off. For a few days, sometimes even a few weeks, we're genuinely committed. And then, slowly, things go back to normal.

So, why does this happen?

I think the biggest reason most New Year's resolutions fail is that we rely too heavily on motivation.

There's something about the beginning of a new year that makes change feel exciting. A fresh calendar, a clean slate, and the feeling that this time things will be different. Motivation is at an all-time high, and suddenly, waking up at 5 AM or going for a run every morning doesn't seem so difficult.

But motivation is an emotion, and like most emotions, it comes and goes.

Eventually, the excitement wears off. You have a long day, it's raining outside, you don't feel like going to the gym, or you simply have other things on your mind. And that's when the real test begins. Unfortunately, most resolutions aren't built to survive those moments.

We often mistake wanting something badly for being prepared to work towards it consistently. The two are very different.

The problem isn't necessarily that we set ambitious goals. It's that we build our plans around the assumption that we'll feel motivated every single day. We forget that progress is rarely exciting. More often than not, it's repetitive, inconvenient, and sometimes downright boring.

I think the solution is to stop treating resolutions as temporary bursts of enthusiasm and start treating them as habits.

Instead of promising to read 30 books in a year, start by reading five pages every day. Instead of committing to an intense workout routine, start with something you can realistically maintain. Make the barrier to starting as small as possible.

And perhaps most importantly, learn to show up even when you don't feel like it.

Missing a day shouldn't mean abandoning the entire goal. One bad week shouldn't become an excuse to give up for the rest of the year.

Ultimately, I don't think the people who achieve their New Year's resolutions are necessarily more motivated than everyone else. They're simply better at continuing when motivation disappears.

Maybe that's what we should focus on this January: not becoming a completely different person overnight, but becoming someone who keeps showing up, even on ordinary days.

# The Resolution That Lasted Has a Witness

Most nights at dinner, my 12-year-old daughter and I check our streaks. We both learn Welsh on an app. I'm on day 700. Neither of us wants to be the one who breaks it, and that, more than anything else, is why the streak is still alive.

I think most New Year's resolutions fail for a boring reason: people lose motivation. That's about it. There's no hidden flaw in the goal and no goal-setting technique they missed. On January 1st you want the thing. By late January you want it a bit less. By March you want it about as much as you did in November, which is to say not enough to do anything about it.

What's interesting is that this is true of everything, including the things that stick. Nobody is motivated to do a language lesson 700 days running. The people who keep going don't feel more than the people who stop. At some point they stop needing to feel anything, because something else is carrying the habit.

In my case, that something is a person. The lesson itself is a few minutes. The part that holds it in place is that someone will ask about it at dinner, every day, and she has a streak of her own to protect, so the asking goes both ways. It's a small, mild, daily pressure. Nothing dramatic. Nobody gets told off. But you'd have to explain why you let it go, out loud, to a twelve-year-old, and that turns out to be enough.

So here's the alternative to willpower. Before you make a resolution, find your witness. Not a coach, not an app that sends you notifications you'll learn to swipe away. A person you already see, ideally one who is trying to keep something going too, so you're checking on each other rather than being supervised. Then put the check somewhere you'll both already be: a meal, a commute, the school run. If it needs its own slot in the week, it'll be the first thing to go.

Motivation is real, and it's great for getting you to January 1st. It just doesn't last, and it was never going to. The question for any resolution isn't "how badly do I want this?" It's "who notices on the day I stop wanting it?"

## **Talk title**

**"AI Should Write More Code. Engineers Should Think More."**

## **5-minute talk outline**

APPROXIMATELY 5 MINUTES · 600–650 WORDS

0:00–0:45

**1. The reality: AI is changing how we build**

Open with a relatable observation: coding assistants can now write functions, debug errors, generate tests and explain unfamiliar code in seconds.

Pose the question: If AI can do all this, should we let it do everything?

0:45–1:45

**2. Where AI genuinely makes us better**

Practical examples:

- Boilerplate code and repetitive tasks.
- Writing unit tests and documentation.
- Understanding unfamiliar codebases.
- Debugging and exploring alternative solutions.

The point: Spend less time on repetitive work and more time solving meaningful problems.

1:45–3:00

**3. The danger of blindly trusting AI**

AI can produce code that looks correct but isn't.

- It can introduce security vulnerabilities.
- It can misunderstand business logic.
- It can create unnecessary complexity.
- It can make developers dependent on suggestions they don't understand.

A particularly relevant example for e-commerce: a seemingly small change to checkout, pricing or inventory logic can have real business consequences.

3:00–4:15

**4. A practical philosophy for using AI**

Establish three principles:

1. **Delegate, don't abdicate:** Let AI do the work, but retain responsibility for the outcome.
2. **Understand before shipping:** Never merge code you cannot explain.
3. **Use judgment:** The higher the business or technical risk, the more carefully AI-generated work should be reviewed and tested.

4:15–5:00

**5. The takeaway**

AI shouldn't make us less capable engineers. It should make us more capable ones.

Close by encouraging experimentation, sharing effective workflows and maintaining accountability.

## **Opening paragraph**

I want to start with a question: how many of us have asked an AI tool to write something for us recently? Maybe it was a piece of code, an email, a spreadsheet formula, or even an idea we weren't quite sure how to approach. The reality is that AI has become incredibly good at taking things that used to require hours of work and getting us 80–90% of the way there in seconds. And that's exciting. But I think there's a question we don't ask ourselves often enough: just because AI *can* do something for us, does that mean we should let it? Today, I want to talk about where AI makes us better at what we do, where it can actually make us worse, and how we can find the balance.

## Outline (5 minutes, ~700 words spoken)

**0:00–0:45 — The incident**
Open on the 2am outage. On-call pastes the error into the assistant. Four tries, four different confident fixes. The problem was in the log; it took about ten minutes to read it and find it. Don't name the engineer. Don't editorialise yet; just tell it the way you'd open a review.

**0:45–1:30 — The pattern, with the number**
This isn't one night. Median time-to-resolve for P2s has gone from 38 minutes to 61 over the last six months. In reviews you keep seeing the same thing: engineers who can't read a stack trace through code they wrote. Say the quote marks out loud: code they "wrote."

**1:30–2:00 — Clear the room's first objection**
This isn't an anti-AI talk. You use it, your team uses it, and for writing new code you're happy with it and not proposing any change. Say that plainly and early so the rest of the talk isn't heard as "AI bad."

**2:00–3:00 — Why debugging is different**
Writing code with an assistant: you review the output, you're still the author. Debugging with one: you paste a symptom and get a plausible story, and the thing you skip is the reading. Reading a trace, reading a log, forming a hypothesis before touching anything. That's the skill that atrophies, and it's the one that doesn't come back from a prompt. The pilot analogy goes here: autopilot is better than the pilot most of the time, and pilots still train on hand-flying, because the day the automation gives you the airplane back is the worst possible day to be learning.

**3:00–4:00 — The proposal**
New engineers: first six months of debugging without an assistant. Not writing code; debugging. Be precise about scope so nobody hears a ban. Address the obvious counter: yes, it will be slower for them for six months. That's the point; you're buying a skill, not shipping fixes faster in month two. Then speak directly to managers: this only works if it's a norm you back, in the moment, when the junior is stuck and the assistant is right there. Say that's the ask.

**4:00–4:45 — What non-engineers should take away**
One line for the rest of the room: nothing is being banned, there is no new policy for the company, this is an engineering norm about how we train people. Then what you'll measure: P2 time-to-resolve, and whether the paste-and-pray pattern shows up in reviews. Report back in six months.

**4:45–5:00 — Close**
Back to 2am. Four confident answers, none of them right, and the real one sitting in the log. The point of the next six months is that the next person on call reads the log first.

## Opening paragraph

A couple of weeks ago we had an outage at two in the morning. The on-call engineer did what most of us would do now: pasted the error into the assistant. It gave a fix. Didn't work. Pasted again. Different fix, just as confident. Four rounds of that. When I got on, I read the log, and it took about ten minutes to find the problem. I'm not telling you this to make anyone look bad, and I'm not telling you it to make the case that AI is bad; I use it every day and so does my whole team. I'm telling you because I run our incident reviews, and this is not a story about one night anymore. Six months ago our median time to resolve a P2 was 38 minutes. It's 61 now. And in review after review I'm watching engineers who can't read a stack trace through code they "wrote." So this is a talk about one specific thing: debugging, and what the assistant is doing to the skill of debugging, and one change I think we should make for the people who are newest here.

# Maybe You Haven't Failed Yet

Every January, millions of people make resolutions. By February, a good number have abandoned them. We call these failed resolutions, talk about a lack of discipline, blame unrealistic expectations, and move on to the next year.

I think we're looking at it all wrong.

We have an odd habit of judging an attempt by its outcome. If you set out to change something and don't manage it, you've failed. But why? Since when did the first attempt have to be the successful one?

I quit smoking on my fourth serious attempt. Six years later, I haven't touched a cigarette.

My first three attempts weren't particularly successful if you measure success by the number of days I stayed away from cigarettes. But each one taught me something.

The second attempt lasted five weeks. I eventually gave in at a wedding. That taught me something important: weddings, drinking and the social environment around them were triggers I hadn't accounted for.

Other attempts revealed different patterns. The first coffee of the morning. Driving. Even spending time with my brother.

By the fourth attempt, I wasn't simply telling myself I was going to quit. I knew what I was up against. I had identified the situations that made it difficult and planned around them.

Six years on, I find it difficult to call those first three attempts failures. Without them, I might never have made the fourth one work.

And this isn't particularly unusual. Research on smoking cessation has consistently found that many successful quitters make several attempts before stopping for good. The journey isn't always a straight line from decision to achievement.

Yet every January, we approach resolutions as though they come with a pass-or-fail deadline.

Perhaps we should stop doing that.

If you decide to exercise regularly and give up after three weeks, that's an attempt. If you try to save money and find yourself back where you started by March, that's an attempt too. The useful question isn't simply why you failed. It's what you discovered that you didn't know before.

What got in the way? What situation caught you off guard? What would you do differently next time?

I'm not suggesting that trying is the same as achieving. It isn't. But treating every unsuccessful attempt as a failure is a pretty good way of ensuring you never learn from it.

So, if your New Year's resolution didn't survive the year, don't just cross it off the list.

Look at what happened. There might be something in there worth taking into your next attempt.

You may not be starting again. You may simply be starting with better information.

## Outline (5 minutes)

**1. The 2am P2 — 0:00 to 0:50**
The opening paragraph below. Four pastes, four confident wrong fixes, ten minutes with the log. Say what you're not here to say: not anti-AI, fine with using it to write code.

**2. What I see from the on-call seat — 0:50 to 1:40**
- Over the last six months, median time-to-resolve on P2s went from 38 minutes to 61.
- In incident reviews, engineers who can't follow a stack trace through code they "wrote."
- Name it precisely: this isn't a code quality problem. The code is mostly fine. It's a debugging problem, and debugging is the one thing the assistant can't do for you on the night the assistant is what's wrong.

**3. Why "use judgment" is how we got here — 1:40 to 2:30** *(the sharp bit)*
- We already have a use-judgment policy. Everyone in this room agrees with it. The number went up anyway.
- Judgment about when to put the tool down is built by debugging without it. Telling a first-year engineer to use judgment assumes they already have the skill the tool is replacing.
- One line to land it: you can't fall back on a skill you never built.

**4. Autopilot — 2:30 to 3:30**
- Pilots fly most of the flight on autopilot. Nobody calls that cheating. They still train manual flying, because the automation hands control back at the worst possible moment, and that's when you need stick-and-rudder.
- 2am with a P2 is the moment the automation hands it back.
- Our version of manual flying is reading a log and a stack trace with nothing but your head.

**5. The proposal — 3:30 to 4:30**
- Juniors: first six months, debugging without an assistant. Write code with it, fine. When something breaks, you read the log, the trace, the code, and you work it. Pair with a senior if you're stuck.
- Be honest about the cost: some fixes will take longer for six months, on a small share of tickets.
- What it buys: an on-call rotation where everyone can find it in ten minutes when the tool is confidently wrong four times in a row.

**6. The ask — 4:30 to 5:00**
- To managers: this needs your sign-off, and I'm asking for it.
- To engineers: I'll keep tracking P2 time-to-resolve and report back in six months. If it doesn't move, I'll say so.
- Close on the number, not a slogan: 38 to 61. I'd like the next number I read out to be going the other way.

## Opening paragraph

We had a P2 go off at two in the morning. The engineer on call did what most of us would do now: pasted the error into the assistant. It came back with a fix, confident, clean. Didn't work. Pasted it again. Different fix, just as confident. Didn't work. Four times, four different answers, none of them right. I got pulled in, opened the log, and found it in about ten minutes. I'm not telling you that to make anyone look bad, and I'm not here to tell you to stop using these tools. I'm not sceptical of them, and I'm fine with people using them to write code. But I run on-call and I run the incident reviews, so I'm the person who sees what happens when the tool is wrong and the human has to take over. What I'm seeing is a skill going away, and I've got five minutes to tell you which one and what I want to do about it.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail (And Maybe It's Not Your Fault)

Every January, we do the same thing. We convince ourselves that this is the year we'll finally get our lives together. We set goals, buy gym memberships, download habit trackers, and promise ourselves that we'll wake up at 5 or 6 AM every morning.

There's just one problem with that advice: it assumes we all live the same life.

Three years in a row, I made the same New Year's resolution. Get to the gym at 6 AM. Three years in a row, I had given up by February.

For a while, I blamed myself. Maybe I wasn't disciplined enough. Maybe I lacked consistency. Maybe I just didn't want it badly enough.

Then I looked at my schedule.

I'm an ER nurse. I rotate between 12-hour day and night shifts every few weeks. A 6 AM gym session sounds great until you've just finished a night shift, haven't slept properly, and your body has absolutely no interest in cooperating.

And that's when it hit me: maybe the problem wasn't my willpower. Maybe the advice was never designed for someone like me.

Most habit-building advice seems to come from the perspective of someone with a predictable 9-to-5 job. Wake up at the same time. Exercise every morning. Follow a routine. Build consistency.

Great advice, if your schedule allows it.

But what about nurses? Warehouse workers? Parents with newborns? Anyone whose working hours, responsibilities, or sleep patterns change constantly?

We keep treating the inability to follow a fixed routine as a personal failure, when the routine itself might be completely unrealistic.

What finally worked for me was changing one thing: I stopped attaching my gym habit to a time and started attaching it to an event.

The gym became the first thing I do after every shift, whether that's a day shift or a night shift. No 6 AM target. No rigid timetable. Just one consistent trigger.

I've kept that going for 14 months now. Something I couldn't sustain for three consecutive Februaries has become part of my life.

So, if your New Year's resolutions keep falling apart, maybe stop asking yourself why you lack discipline. Start asking whether the system you're trying to follow actually fits your life.

Find an anchor that works with your schedule, not against it. It could be after a shift, after dropping the kids off, or before heading home.

Your routine doesn't have to look like everyone else's to work.

And honestly, that's probably the point.

## Outline (5 minutes)

**1. The number (0:00–0:45)** — opening paragraph below. Two figures, no setup: tests went 2,000 → 9,000 in a year, nightly went 20 min → 3 hours.

**2. What that number is and isn't (0:45–1:45)**
- It isn't a story about AI writing bad tests. The tests pass. They're probably individually fine.
- It's a story about what nobody asked: does this test fail on anything the existing ones don't? My read, as the person staring at the run every morning, is that for most of the new 7,000 the answer is no.
- The tool did exactly what it was asked. "Write tests for this" became 30 tests where 3 would have done, because 30 cost the same as 3.
- Say plainly: this is a guess until we measure it. (Insert the coverage comparison if you ran it.)

**3. Why I'm talking about tests and not features (1:45–2:45)**
- Tests are just where the cost is visible: a 3-hour nightly is a number on a dashboard. The same thing is almost certainly happening in places with no dashboard — config, helpers, docs, retry logic, abstractions that exist because generating them was free.
- "Everything" doesn't mean the assistant writes everything. In practice it means the assistant *decides what gets written*, by making volume free. Volume isn't free downstream: someone runs it, reads it, waits for it, debugs it when it flakes.
- The judgment the tool can't do for you isn't "is this code right," it's "should this code be here."

**4. The norm (2:45–4:00)**
- Proposal, starting with tests because that's my patch: **a test gets merged with one line saying what would now fail that didn't before.** If you can't write that line, the test doesn't go in.
- Second half: **nightly runtime becomes a tracked number with an owner** (me), and it doesn't go up without a reason that's written down.
- Why this and not "use AI less": the norm is about the question, not the tool. Use the assistant for all of it if you like; just answer the question before merge. Most of the time the answer takes ten seconds.
- For the PMs in the room: this is the same discipline you apply to a backlog. More tickets isn't more product.

**5. Close (4:00–5:00)**
- Offer: I'll run the coverage comparison and the first prune of the suite in the next sprint and report what 7,000 tests were actually buying us. Then we can decide whether the norm goes beyond tests.
- Last line: the assistants are good enough that "can it write this" is settled. The only question left is the one we were supposed to be asking all along — "does this need to exist" — and the suite says we've stopped asking it.

---

## Opening paragraph

> A year ago our test suite had about 2,000 tests in it. Today it has about 9,000. The nightly run that used to take 20 minutes now takes three hours. Most of those new tests were written by an AI assistant, and I want to be clear up front: they pass. They're not broken. If you opened one at random you'd probably say it looks fine. I'm the QA lead, so that suite is my problem, and here's what I think the extra 7,000 tests are mostly doing: checking the same things the first 2,000 already checked. That's a guess, and I'll tell you how I'd prove it. But I'd rather start there than with the question I was given, which was whether engineers should use these tools for everything. Because I think the suite already answered it. The tools wrote exactly what they were asked to. What got skipped was the ten seconds where someone asks whether it needed writing at all.

## **5-minute all-hands outline**

**Title: AI Can Write the Code. Who Owns It?**

TARGET LENGTH · 5 MINUTES · APPROX. 600 WORDS

### **1. Opening: The August incident (0:00–0:50)**

- Start with the AI-generated database migration.
- It silently dropped a NOT NULL constraint.
- The result was a reconciliation mismatch that took three weeks to trace.
- The engineer who merged it couldn't explain what the migration actually did.
- Establish the point: the problem wasn't that AI wrote the code. It was that someone merged code they didn't understand.

### **2. The economics of AI-assisted engineering (0:50–1:45)**

Use your own numbers:

- PR volume has increased approximately 60% since spring.
- New hires are ramping up roughly twice as fast.
- That's genuinely good. AI is making us faster and more capable.
- But senior engineers' review time has increased from approximately 4 to 11 hours per week each.

**The key observation:** We have reduced the cost of producing code, but increased the cost of verifying it. That cost is disproportionately landing on two senior engineers.

### **3. The principle: You own every line (1:45–3:00)**

Make this the central message.

- It doesn't matter whether you wrote the code, Copilot wrote it, or Claude wrote it.
- If your name is on the PR, you own the code.
- "The AI wrote it" is never an acceptable explanation in a postmortem.
- You should be able to explain what your code does, why it does it, and what could go wrong.
- Generating code is not the same as engineering.

### **4. What changes from here (3:00–4:15)**

Keep this practical and specific.

Three expectations:

1. **Understand before you merge.** If you cannot explain a change, you aren't ready to approve it.
2. **Respect review capacity.** PRs exceeding 400 changed lines get split. Large AI-generated diffs aren't a shortcut around review.
3. **Don't outsource judgment.** AI can generate implementations, tests, migrations, and suggestions. The engineer remains responsible for correctness and consequences.

### **5. Closing: The standard we want (4:15–5:00)**

- We aren't going backwards. AI is here to stay.
- We want new hires ramping faster and engineers spending less time on repetitive work.
- But we cannot achieve that by transferring the burden to the people reviewing everyone else's output.
- The goal isn't to maximise lines of code or PR volume.
- The goal is to ship reliable software, faster, without sacrificing accountability.

End with:

**"Use AI as much as you want. Just never use it as an excuse for not knowing what you've shipped."**

## Opening paragraph

In August, a change went into our database. It was small, it was written by an AI assistant, and it went in the way changes go in. What it did, and nobody noticed at the time, was quietly remove a rule that said one particular field could never be left empty. That's it. One safety check, gone. For the next three weeks, numbers that were supposed to match stopped matching, and it took that long to trace it back to that one change. When we did, we asked the engineer who'd merged it what the change did. And they couldn't say. I'm not telling you this to point at anyone. I'm telling you because I think that sentence, "I can't say what it did," is the real problem, and it has very little to do with how much AI our engineers are using. So I'm not going to spend five minutes on pros and cons. I'm going to tell you what's changed since the spring, and then ask you to back three rules.

# My 6am Gym Habit Died Every February. The Clock Killed It.

Three Januaries in a row I resolved to be at the gym at 6am. Three Februaries in a row it was dead. Not because I stopped wanting it. Because the rotation flipped me to nights, and 6am stopped meaning anything. It was the middle of a shift, or the hour I was finally getting to sleep, or some fog in between. The habit didn't quit. The clock it was tied to stopped existing.

If you work rotating 12s, you already know this feeling. You read the same resolution advice as everyone else: "same time every day," "build a morning routine," "lay your clothes out the night before." And you think, which night? Which morning? Your week has two of each, in the wrong order.

Here's what I've landed on: most New Year's resolutions don't fail on willpower. They fail because almost all the advice is written by and for people with a 9-to-5. "Same time every day" works beautifully when every day is the same shape. For a nurse on rotating 12s, for warehouse staff, for the parent of a newborn, there is no "every day." There's just whatever the schedule did to you this week.

So I stopped anchoring to a clock and anchored to an event. The gym is the first thing I do after any shift ends. Days, nights, doesn't matter. The shift ends, I go. Fourteen months and counting, which is fourteen months longer than the 6am version ever managed.

Nothing about this is simple. Walking into a gym after twelve hours on your feet is not simple. But it's possible, which 6am on a night rotation never was. The rule finally fits the life, instead of the life having to bend around the rule.

So if yours died last February too, stop reading that as a verdict on your discipline. Look at what it was tied to. If it was a time of day, and your days don't come in a fixed shape, it was never going to survive the first rotation change. Find the thing that happens no matter what shape the day takes, and hang the habit on that. For us it's clocking out. For you it might be the kid going down, or the end of a route.

The office people can keep their morning routines. We get to build something that survives nights.

# Count attempts, not outcomes

Attempt two died at a wedding.

Five weeks in, I was fine. Then: drinks, everyone outside smoking, and that was it. Back on a pack a day inside a week.

By the usual scoring, that's a failed resolution. One attempt, one outcome, file it. Most New Year's resolutions get scored exactly like this, which is why "most resolutions fail" is a statistic everyone nods at and nobody learns anything from.

The frame is wrong. It treats one attempt as the whole experiment.

I smoked for fifteen years. I quit on my fourth serious attempt, and I've been clean for six. Attempts one through three failed. That isn't a 25% success rate. It's one quit that took four tries, which is how quitting smoking usually goes. Most people who get there needed several runs at it. The studies disagree on how many; none of them say one.

Here's what the failed attempts actually were.

Attempt one taught me about the first coffee of the day. Attempt three taught me about driving, and about my brother. Attempt two taught me weddings and alcohol. Each one found a trigger I didn't know I had, or didn't want to know I had. Each one ended at exactly the point where I'd have needed a plan and didn't have one.

Attempt four was planned around those things. Not around willpower, not around a date. Around first coffee, driving, my brother, drinks, weddings. The five things that had already beaten me three times.

It held. Not because I was stronger that year. Because I finally had the information.

That's what "resolutions fail" hides. The failures aren't the opposite of the success. They're the raw material for it. A quit that ends at week five isn't the experiment failing. It's the experiment returning a result: here is where it breaks.

Count outcomes and you get a string of zeros and a story about yourself. Count attempts and you get a list of conditions, and the next attempt starts where the last one stopped.

So, one move. Not a list.

When an attempt ends, write down what broke it. Not "I was weak." The actual conditions: where you were, what you'd had, who was there, what time of day. Then plan the next attempt around exactly that, and nothing else.

The resolution didn't fail. It came back with a finding. Use it.

## **2. Opening paragraph**

I want to start with a situation I think most of us have experienced by now. You open Cursor, Claude, or whichever AI coding assistant you prefer, describe what you want to build, and within a few seconds, you have 100 lines of code sitting in front of you. It looks clean, it looks convincing, and for a moment, you feel incredibly productive. And honestly, you probably are. But here's something I've been thinking about: **just because AI can write code faster than we can, does that necessarily mean we're building better software?** I don't think the answer is always yes, and I think that's a conversation worth having.

## **3. Three key arguments to develop**

I'd keep coming back to these throughout the speech.

**Argument 1: AI is an accelerator, not a replacement for judgement.**

- Use it for boilerplate, repetitive tasks, debugging, documentation and exploring unfamiliar code.
- Let it save time on things that don't require your deepest thinking.
- But don't let it make decisions you don't understand.

**Argument 2: The speed-quality trade-off is real.**

- Code that compiles isn't necessarily good code.
- Code that passes a test isn't necessarily robust code.
- AI can introduce unnecessary abstractions, overlooked edge cases and subtle bugs.
- The faster we generate code, the more important thoughtful reviews become.

**Argument 3: Ownership doesn't transfer to AI.**

- If AI writes the code, the engineer still owns the outcome.
- You should be able to explain what the code does and why it works.
- You should be comfortable questioning or rejecting its suggestions.
- Particularly in insurance software, a small defect can have consequences beyond a failed feature.

## **4. The closing thought**

I'd finish with something conversational rather than overly motivational:

I don't think the solution is to use AI less. If anything, I think we should be experimenting with it more. The opportunity is enormous, and I don't think we should ignore it. But I do think we need to change how we measure productivity. It's not about how many lines of code we can generate, how quickly we can close a ticket, or how much work we can delegate to an AI assistant. It's about whether we're actually building better, more reliable software. So my take is simple: use AI, challenge it, learn from it, and let it make you faster. But never switch off your engineering judgement. Because at the end of the day, AI might write the code, but we're still responsible for what we ship.

I've got five minutes, so I'll be direct. The question on the slide is whether engineers should use AI coding assistants for everything, and I think that's the wrong question, because we've already answered it. Nobody decided. It just happened. Some of us use Copilot for most of what we write, some of us don't touch it, and there's no policy, no conversation, nothing written down anywhere. That's worked well enough so far, and I'm not up here to say stop. I'm up here to say the part we skipped. Using these tools is easy. The thing nobody has said out loud is that when you put your name on a pull request, you own every line in it, including the ones you didn't type. If you can't explain what a block does and why it's there, it isn't ready to merge, whoever or whatever wrote it. For the engineers in the room, that's a working habit. For everyone else, it's the answer to "are we getting faster or just sloppier": we get faster, as long as we hold that line.

**The resolution didn't fail. The clock did.**

Three Januaries in a row I resolved to be at the gym at 6am. Three Februaries in a row the rotation flipped and the habit died. Not because I stopped wanting it. Because 6am stopped being a time I could reliably be anywhere.

The usual reading of that is a willpower story. You wanted it in January; by February you didn't want it enough. Every article about why resolutions fail lands on some version of this, and then hands you the cure: same time every day, build a morning routine, stack it onto your coffee.

Read that advice again and notice who it's for. Same time every day. Morning routine. It assumes a life where Monday looks like Tuesday, where "morning" is a fixed thing that happens once per day at a predictable hour. That's a real life. A lot of people have it. Most of the people reading this don't.

Nurses, warehouse staff, anyone with a newborn: your week doesn't have a shape, it has a roster. The one ingredient the advice depends on, a stable clock, is the one ingredient you can't supply. So you build the plan on a time, the roster moves the time, the plan collapses, and then you get told it's a discipline problem. It isn't. It's a calendar problem wearing a discipline costume.

What finally stuck for me wasn't more resolve. It was changing what the habit was attached to. Gym is the first thing after any shift ends. Day shift, night shift, doesn't matter. Shift ends, gym. The rotation can flip as often as it likes; "after shift" still exists every single week, because a shift ending is something that happens to me regardless of what the clock says. Fourteen months now. 6am turned out to be a lovely idea for someone else.

The difference is small on paper and enormous in practice. A time belongs to your roster. An event belongs to you. Anchor a habit to a time and you've handed its survival to whoever writes the schedule. Anchor it to something that happens anyway, end of shift, the handover, the drive home, and it goes wherever your week goes.

So if you're about to write a resolution for January, don't pick a time. Pick a thing that already happens in your week no matter what the week looks like, and put the new thing right after it. The resolution was never the problem.

# The Skill We Can't Afford to Lose

*Five-minute all-hands talk*

## 1. The opening: AI is genuinely making us better (0:00–0:45)

**Opening paragraph:**

I want to start by saying something that might sound contradictory given the title of this talk: I think AI coding assistants are one of the best things to happen to engineering in years. I use them myself. They help us move faster, explore ideas we might otherwise not have had time to explore, and take care of work that doesn't necessarily require our deepest attention. And in a business like ours, where the systems we build determine whether trucks move, whether deliveries happen and whether customers can trust us, that kind of leverage matters. But I think there's a question we're not asking enough: as we get better at making machines do the work, are we getting worse at understanding the work ourselves?

## 2. What we're getting right, and what we might be losing (0:45–1:30)

Acknowledge the genuine benefits:

- Faster development and prototyping.
- Less time spent on repetitive coding.
- More room to focus on architecture and higher-value problems.
- Better leverage for engineers across the organisation.

Then introduce the distinction:

There is a difference between being able to produce code and being able to understand a system.

AI can help us produce code. But when something breaks at 2am, we need engineers who understand what they're looking at.

Our responsibility isn't just to ship features. It's to keep the business running.

## 3. The signal we're seeing (1:30–2:30)

Bring in the data:

Over the last six months, our median time-to-resolve for P2 incidents has increased from 38 minutes to 61 minutes.

That's a roughly 61% increase.

Be careful not to claim AI caused this. There could be multiple contributing factors. But it is a signal worth investigating.

Then share what you're seeing in incident reviews:

- Engineers struggling to read stack traces.
- Difficulty tracing an error through code they helped write.
- Less confidence in reasoning through a problem without immediately asking an assistant.

The important point:

This isn't about engineers being less capable. It's about the habits we're building as an organisation.

## 4. The 2am incident (2:30–3:30)

Tell the story without identifying the engineer.

One night, we had an outage. The on-call engineer was trying to resolve it and did what many of us would instinctively do: pasted the error into an AI assistant.

Four times.

Four different answers. Four confident suggested fixes.

Meanwhile, the actual problem was sitting in the logs. It took roughly ten minutes of reading through them to identify what was happening.

The lesson isn't that the engineer shouldn't have used AI. The lesson is that when the tool couldn't reliably diagnose the issue, we needed someone who could reason independently.

**The dangerous situation isn't an AI giving us a wrong answer. It's an engineer not knowing how to recognise that the answer is wrong.**

## 5. The aviation analogy (3:30–4:15)

Think about commercial aviation.

Modern aircraft have extraordinarily sophisticated autopilot systems. Pilots don't spend every flight manually controlling every aspect of the aircraft.

But pilots still train to fly manually.

Why?

Because automation handles the routine. Human skill matters when the routine breaks down.

You don't learn to hand-fly a plane because you expect to do it every day. You learn because when automation hands you a mess at the worst possible moment, you need to know how to fly.

Engineering is no different.

AI should be our autopilot, not our replacement for understanding how to fly.

## 6. The concrete ask (4:15–4:45)

Here's what I'd like us to consider:

For the first six months of a junior engineer's career, let them use AI to write code, explore solutions and accelerate development.

But ask them to debug without an AI assistant.

Let them read the logs, trace the stack, understand the failure and explain the root cause themselves before turning to an assistant.

Managers should support this as a deliberate training practice, not treat it as a productivity penalty.

This isn't about making people slower. It's about building the foundational skills that make them effective when things go wrong.

## 7. Closing (4:45–5:00)

I don't want us to become an organisation that is slower because it refuses to use AI.

I want us to become an organisation that can move faster because it knows when to use AI, when to question it, and when it needs a human who genuinely understands the system.

**Let's make sure we're building engineers who can use the autopilot, but can still fly the plane.**

## Opening paragraph

A year ago our test suite had about 2,000 tests. Today it has about 9,000. Most of the new ones were written with an AI assistant, and nearly all of them pass. Over the same year the nightly run went from twenty minutes to three hours. I'm fairly sure a lot of those tests check the same things — not because anyone was careless, but because when writing a test costs nothing, nobody opens the file to see what's already there. That's the version of the AI question I want to talk about. Not "is the code good," because mostly it is. The question is what happens when producing code gets cheap and everything after producing it doesn't.

**Resolutions don't fail. They get forgotten.**

I've made New Year's resolutions. I couldn't tell you what most of them were. That's not quite the same as failing at them. Failing would mean I tried, hit something hard, and stopped. What actually happened is that they drifted off sometime in January and I didn't notice they were gone.

I think that's the usual story, and I think it says something about where resolutions come from.

Most of them come from the date. The year is ending, there's a general feeling that something should be reviewed and improved, and so you produce a goal to fill the slot. The goal might be a perfectly good one. But the thing that made you say it out loud was the calendar, not anything in your life. Nothing changed on December 31st except the number.

That matters, because the date is the one part of a resolution that doesn't last. By the second week of January it's just a Tuesday. Whatever energy came from the sense of a fresh start is gone, because the start isn't fresh anymore. If the resolution was borrowed from that feeling, there's nothing left holding it up. It doesn't break. It just has no reason to still be there.

Compare that with the changes that actually stick. People tend to make them at odd times: a doctor says something, a job ends, someone moves, a bad night turns into a decision. The timing is ugly and the change is specific, because it's an answer to something real. Nobody forgets a decision they made because they had to. You forget the ones you made because it was the right week to make one.

This is why the usual advice doesn't quite reach the problem. Make it smaller, make it specific, attach it to a habit. All sensible. But it treats the problem as one of design, and I think it's mostly one of origin. A well-designed resolution with no reason behind it is still a resolution with no reason behind it. You've built a better container for something that was never going to be there in February.

None of this means January is a bad time to change something. It means the date shouldn't be the reason. If there's something you'd want to do anyway, and it happens to be December, fine. If you're reaching for a goal because the year is ending and it feels like you should have one, that's the kind I've made before, and I couldn't tell you how any of them ended, because they didn't end. They were just gone.

**Count the attempts**

Every January someone writes that most New Year's resolutions fail. The numbers vary, the conclusion doesn't: people set goals, people quit, the gym empties out by February.

The frame is wrong. Most attempts fail. That's not the same thing, and the difference matters.

I smoked for fifteen years. I quit on my fourth serious attempt, and I've been clean for six. By the usual way of counting, the first three attempts were failures. Three resolutions, three collapses. That's the story the "most resolutions fail" articles would tell about me, right up until the fourth one happened to stick.

But that isn't what happened. Attempt two lasted five weeks and broke at a wedding. Counted as an outcome, that's five weeks of work gone over one evening. Counted as anything else, it was information. Weddings and drinking were my trigger. I didn't know that going in, and nothing short of standing at a wedding with a drink in my hand was going to tell me. By attempt four I knew, and attempt four was planned around exactly that.

The same goes for the rest. The first three attempts, between them, taught me where the cigarette actually lived: the first coffee, driving, and my brother. Not "stress", not "habit". Those three specific things. I didn't know those going in either. The attempts found them. Attempt four wasn't a better resolution. It was the same resolution with three attempts' worth of data behind it.

So here's the counting mistake. If you count outcomes, I failed three times and succeeded once. If you count attempts, I made four, each better informed than the last, and the fourth closed it out. Most people who quit smoking for good needed several tries. That isn't a sign their resolution was weak. It's how it normally goes.

This changes what a broken attempt means. It doesn't mean you lacked willpower, and it doesn't mean the resolution was wrong. It means you now know something you couldn't have learned any other way: the exact situation that gets you. Write it down. Next attempt, that situation is the thing you plan around.

Most resolutions don't fail. Most attempts do, and the resolution is what's left standing across them. If your January attempt breaks, look at where it broke. That's the whole point of it.
